User: How can elementary students create their own character poem using Roald Dahl's poetry as an example?: Students will enjoy analyzing the exuberant poems of Roald Dahl. His creative rhymes are an intrinsic part of his classic stories. They add a wacky break in the story line, while giving insight into the character or situation at hand. Roald Dahl poems pepper his books such as; The Witches, Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and James and the Giant Peach play an integral part in the stories.
Roald Dahl was very kind to English teachers when he wrote the many lines of verse. His poetry follows classic patterns, making it easy to incorporate his works into any study of poetry.
For this lesson, I used the book Vile Verses, an anthology of Roald Dahl’s poetry from his books, as well as poems that were previously unpublished. He was a prolific writer who also retold nursery rhymes and described animals with a very different point of view.
For this two part study for elementary students, wake the students up by reciting, Down With Children from The Witches. This silly poem is a fantastic way to get their attention and teach the concept of rhyming couplets.
Couplets are made up of two lines. At the end of the lines are words that rhyme and the two lines together make a complete thought.
Have the students pick out the rhyming couplets that Roald Dahl used; in, skin, mash, bash, louder, powder, trice, mice and so on.
Ask the class to brainstorm their own collection of rhyming words. Keeping a running list in a poetry notebook is a good idea for future lessons.
Work on a building a piece of poetry using couplets that the students come up with.
Once the class gets the concept of rhyming couplets down, introduce another Roald Dahl poem such as this one from Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, Concerning Veronica Salt.This poem also makes good use of rhyming couplets and can be used as another excellent example, although for this lesson focus on Character poetry.
Start by breaking the students into work groups of four or five.
Recite the poem to the class, have handouts of the poem, if possible, to give to each group.
Let them pick out the rhyming words in this poem and copy into their poetry notebook as a reference. Have the groups share the rhyming words they have previously come up with as well.
Now, invite the groups to come up with a character.
They will start by deciding if it will be a boy or girl, man or woman.
What are the faults of this person? Describe them with lots of expression.
Exaggerate how they look, talk and walk.
How do they like to spend their time?
One of the students from each group can be the designated artist and draw the character as it is described.
Have the groups put their thoughts together into couplets individually.
Then let them string the couplets together to create a unique character poem.
Roald Dahl poems will get reluctant writers to the page. Try incorporating his verse whenever your lessons start to get a little stale and watch the class perk up.
Agent: Here is an example of a character poem that students could create using the above instructions:

Meet Sally Sue, a girl so bold,
Her hair's the color of marigold.
But watch out, don't make her mad,
Or she'll throw a fit and then get sad.

Her voice is loud, her laugh is strong,
She dances all day long.
But when it's time to do her chores,
She stomps her feet and she ignores.

Sally's stubborn, that's for sure,
She wants her way, nothing more.
But underneath it all, she cares,
And that's what makes her, Sally, rare.

User: Can you give some tips on how to help students come up with descriptive language for their character poems?
Agent: Certainly! Here are some tips on how to help students come up with descriptive language for their character poems:

1. Brainstorm adjectives: Have students brainstorm a list of descriptive adjectives that they could use to describe their character. Encourage them to think outside the box and come up with unique and interesting adjectives.

2. Use the senses: Encourage students to use sensory details in their character poems. For example, they could describe how their character smells, sounds, tastes, looks, and feels.

3. Consider the character's actions: Think about what the character does and how they do it. Use action verbs and descriptive language to show how the character moves, talks, and interacts with others.

4. Show, don't tell: Encourage students to use descriptive language to show their character's personality rather than just telling the reader what their personality is like. For example, instead of saying "My character is brave," they could show the character doing something brave.

5. Use figurative language: Encourage students to use similes, metaphors, and other types of figurative language in their character poems. This can help to make the language more descriptive and interesting.

By using these tips, students should be able to come up with descriptive and engaging language for their character poems.

Answer according to: Great news for “go local” businesses: more than 85 percent of brand engagement by consumers is through local listings, web pages and search results, Search Engine Land reports. More than 60 percent of people research products online before purchasing, according to Nielsen research, so there are plenty of opportunities to turn a local search interaction into a purchase. Here’s how.
With Google searches accounting for nearly three-quarters of all search engine queries, building a local search strategy with Google is essential. Google My Business is a business feature for brick and mortars to use to showcase hours, add photos, respond to user reviews on Google and more. When customers search for a business using Google or Maps, the Google My Business result is prominently shown. Proactively managing this result can help a business control how it appears to users who search.
Use Google My Business insights to see how customers are interacting with your brand, such as if they’re requesting directions, visiting your website or calling you from the listing. Data like this can help you optimize customer interactions, such as leaving directions in a voicemail greeting, or making sure you train more staff members to answer phones and complete actions on calls. You can also see which photos are most popular, where customers are requesting directions from and more.
The more reviews a local business has and the higher-rated the reviews are on Google, the more likely a business is to appear in top results for general searches, such as the top three restaurants that appear for an “Italian food Denver” search, reports Denver digital marketing agency AlphaMind Studios. Make sure you mention how great it’d be for your happy customers to leave you a Google review, and post a call to action to review your business on Google to increase your number of high-quality reviews.
Depending on your industry, there are many other search directories you should have a presence on. Think beyond local. For example, someone might search, “Phoenix plumbing companies Angie’s List”, pairing a nationwide directory with a local city in a single search.

Optimize your pages. Take the same care with local listings that you would your own website. Claim vanity urls. On sites like Facebook where you can create a custom url with your brand name in it, do so. This makes you more searchable in search engines and helps you protect your brand.

User: How can I make a healthy meal plan on a budget?
Agent: 1. Plan Ahead: Plan your meals in advance to save money and reduce food waste. Look for recipes that use similar ingredients so you can buy in bulk.

2. Shop Sales: Check the sales flyers for your local grocery store to see what is on sale that week. Try to plan your meals around those items.

3. Buy In Season: Produce that is in season is usually less expensive and fresher than produce that is out of season. Plan your meals around what is in season.

4. Use Coupons: Use coupons and discounts to save money on groceries.

5. Buy Store Brand: Often, store-brand items are just as good as name-brand items but are less expensive.

6. Cook at Home: Cooking at home is usually less expensive than eating out. Cook large batches of food to have leftovers for later in the week.

7. Eat Less Meat: Meat is usually more expensive than vegetables and grains. Consider having vegetarian meals or using meat as a condiment rather than the main course.

8. Use the Freezer: Freeze leftover food or buy items in bulk and freeze them for later use.

9. Limit Processed Foods: Processed foods are usually more expensive and less healthy than whole foods.

10. Cut Out Extras: Skip the expensive drinks, snacks, and desserts to save money and eat healthier.

User: These recipe ideas sound great! I'm excited to try the baked sweet potato chips. Any tips on getting them crispy?
Agent: Yes! Here are some tips for getting crispy baked sweet potato chips:

1. Slice the Sweet Potatoes Thinly: The thinner the slices, the crispier the chips will be. Try to cut them as thinly and evenly as possible so that they bake evenly.

2. Soak the Sliced Potatoes in Water: Soaking them in water for 15-30 minutes before baking removes excess starch and makes them crispier.

3. Dry the Sweet Potatoes Thoroughly: Pat the slices dry with a paper towel to remove as much moisture as possible before baking. Moisture can prevent them from getting crispy.

4. Use Parchment Paper: The chips will stick to the baking sheet without parchment paper, so using it will help them to crisp up nicely.

5. Use High Heat: Baking the chips at a high temperature - around 400°F - helps them to get crispy. Keep a close eye on them as they can burn quickly at such high heat.

6. Flip the Chips: Halfway through baking, flip the chips over to ensure even crisping.

Enjoy your crispy baked sweet potato chips!

The first inkling I had that there was more to at-home cooking than bland, quick and easy-to-make meals was when I would eat with my post-college boyfriend (my now-husband) and his medical school roommates. They didn’t use recipes and certainly didn’t read instructions the rare times they used anything pre-made. Nic, AJ and Chris would throw things from the fridge directly into a big pan, and would then create some sort of sauce to go with it from whatever liquids they had on hand. They used herbs, REAL garlic (up to this point I thought garlic was a powder that you would buy in the spice aisle), and all manners of fresh vegetables. It was inspired chaos and it was delicious. I loved the by-product of these kitchen sessions, but their cooking methods really stressed me out. If I didn’t know how to cook a meal by heart, I would HAVE to have instructions and would HAVE to follow them step-by-step. It dawned on me that if I had skills, knowledge, and confidence in my cooking abilities I’d be able to cook more freely. So I began to take cooking classes. The beauty of cooking classes is that you learn a whole host of skills while enjoying delicious food and unique cocktails. It ends up being just a really fun, educational experience. I took my first classes in San Diego in Pacific Beach at Great News. I took observational classes, where the chef prepares the meal while teaching knife skills, cooking techniques, shortcuts, and easy variations to the recipes they shared. In San Francisco there are several cooking schools that are highly recommended. I took a page from Julia Child and took my first class in SOMA at Le Cordon Bleu. Le Cordon Bleu is a professional cooking school but they also offer classes for non-professionals. My husband and I took a “Home for the Holidays” class the weekend before Thanksgiving so that we were prepared to host our first Thanksgiving meal. This was the first hands-on class I have taken and I really enjoyed it. The Chef started us off by teaching the preparation of the main dish, Turkey Ballentine. Then we all went to stations and prepared the other side dishes for the meal. We were stuck chopping and peeling vegetables for the Ginger Apple Butternut Squash Bisque for a bit at our station, but as soon as we finished we were able to follow the chef around station by station and learned knife skills, cooking chemistry, and helpful tricks. At the end of the morning we all sat down and enjoyed the Thanksgiving feast we had each played a part in. We were also able to take home some of the incredible Turkey Giblet Gravy that the chef himself had whipped up out of a home-made turkey stock, roux, and a savory mixture of herbs. ~ by jessicamoriates on December 5, 2010. Agent: One summer, I decided to take a solo trip to South Africa. I had always been fascinated by the country's rich history and diverse culture, but I knew very little about it beyond what I had learned in textbooks. I was excited to discover something new, but I was also nervous about navigating a foreign land alone.

As soon as I stepped off the plane, I was hit by the bright, hot sun and the intense energy of the city of Johannesburg. My preconceptions of South Africa as a strife-ridden, poverty-stricken country were immediately challenged by the vibrant, bustling streets and colorful markets. I quickly realized that my experience was going to be far from what I had anticipated.

Over the course of my trip, I traveled to several cities and towns, speaking with locals and immersing myself in their daily lives. I visited a number of historical sites, such as the Apartheid Museum and the Hector Pieterson Memorial, both of which provided a stark reminder of the country's troubled past. However, I was also struck by the resilience and hope of the people I met, who had overcome unimaginable obstacles to build a new, more inclusive society.

As I navigated the country, I learned a great deal about myself. I came to appreciate the value of stepping outside of my comfort zone and embracing new experiences. I learned to trust my instincts and embrace uncertainty, even when it felt uncomfortable or scary. I discovered a newfound sense of courage and self-reliance, as I navigated unfamiliar streets and interacted with strangers in a foreign language.

Of course, there were obstacles along the way. At times, I felt lost and overwhelmed, unsure of how to navigate the complexities of this new culture. I encountered language barriers and cultural misunderstandings, and I struggled with feelings of homesickness and loneliness. However, as I pushed through these challenges, I gained strength and resilience, emerging from the experience with a newfound sense of confidence and self-assurance.

Looking back on my trip to South Africa, I am incredibly grateful for the lessons I learned and the experiences I had. I will always remember the bright colors and smells of the local markets, the sound of drumming at a traditional Zulu ceremony, and the feel of the warm sand beneath my feet as I walked along a pristine beach. But more than anything else, I will remember the sense of discovery and growth that came from stepping outside of my comfort zone and embracing the unknown.

The exploitative economic practices of colonialism often led to poverty, inequality, and environmental destruction in the colonies. Some British colonial policies also exacerbated conflict and tension between different ethnic and religious groups within the colonies, leading to problems that persist until today.

Overall, the economic motivations behind British colonialism played a significant role in shaping the colonies and their relationship with the British Empire. While British colonialism had some positive impacts on the colonies, it also had many negative consequences that continue to be felt today.
